title: Circuit Breakers & Bulkheads
subtitle: Watch one slow dependency drain a whole service, then watch a breaker, a bulkhead and a fallback stop it.
learn: Why a slow dependency is more dangerous than a dead one
How a circuit breaker moves between closed, open and half-open
How failing fast frees threads and gives the sick service room to recover
How bulkheads cap the damage one dependency can do to shared pools
How to pick a fallback that degrades the page instead of breaking it

steps.title: A nice-to-have takes down the page
steps.body: A shop's product page calls two services. Recommendations is the 'you may also like' row, a nice-to-have. Payments is essential. The Shop API handles 500 requests per second with 200 worker threads (a thread handles one request at a time). Recommendations normally answers in 40 ms, so about 20 threads wait on it at any moment (500 x 0.04 s), plus a couple for other work: 22 busy. A thin wrapper sits in between, a plain pass-through for now. What happens when that one optional service stops answering?
steps.idea: A dependency you could live without can still sink you if you keep waiting on it.
steps.caption: Healthy baseline: 500 req/s, about 22 busy threads.

steps.title: Slow is worse than down
steps.body: Recommendations now hangs for 30 seconds before failing. A crashed service usually refuses connections instantly, so the caller moves on. A hung one holds a thread until a timeout fires. By Little's law (calls in progress = arrival rate x time each takes), 500 per second x 30 seconds wants 15,000 threads, but we only have 200. The pool is full in under half a second. Now even checkout, which never needed recommendations, queues for a thread and fails with 503.
steps.idea: Slow calls hold resources. Running out of them turns one sick dependency into a full outage, called a cascading failure.
steps.caption: Threads pile up waiting on Recommendations, so checkout fails too.

steps.title: Closed: counting quietly
steps.body: Let us rewind to the healthy moment to see what a circuit breaker does normally. It is a small wrapper around calls to one dependency. Like an electrical breaker, 'closed' means current flows: every call goes through. The breaker watches recent results in a rolling window (say the last 10 seconds) and counts failures and timeouts. In this normal state it costs almost nothing, just a counter.
steps.idea: Closed is the normal state: pass everything through and keep score.
steps.caption: Breaker closed: calls pass, outcomes are counted.

steps.title: Trip: closed becomes open
steps.body: Now Recommendations hangs again. Suppose the rule is: once the window holds at least 20 calls, trip if 50% or more failed. A short per-call timeout (500 ms here) turns each hang into a counted failure. It takes a few seconds for enough failures to pile up, so the breaker trips soon, not instantly. A timeout alone cannot save us: 500 calls/s x 0.5 s is about 250 calls in flight, more than 200 threads. Once the limit is crossed, the breaker opens. These numbers are rules of thumb you tune from real traffic.
steps.idea: A timeout makes slowness countable. The failure-rate threshold decides when to trip.
steps.caption: Failures cross 50%: the breaker trips open.

steps.title: Open: reject in a millisecond
steps.body: While open, the breaker does not call Recommendations at all. It answers at once with an error the Shop API can handle. Each request now holds a thread for about a millisecond instead of 500 ms or more, so busy threads fall to just a few. Page errors drop as the last hung calls drain, and the row is simply left out until the next step adds a fallback. The sick service also stops getting 500 calls per second, which gives it quiet time to recover.
steps.idea: Failing fast protects the caller's threads and gives the sick service room to heal.
steps.caption: Calls rejected locally; Recommendations is left alone.

steps.title: Degrade instead of erroring
steps.body: A rejected call still needs an answer. For optional data, the breaker's fallback (a backup answer) returns a cached list of the 20 most popular items, refreshed every few minutes. Shoppers see a slightly less personal row and nothing else changes. Pick fallbacks that are cheap and do not depend on the failing service: a cache, a default value, or hiding the widget. Never fall back to calling another fragile service.
steps.idea: Graceful degradation: return a worse answer instead of no answer.
steps.caption: Breaker serves popular items from cache.

steps.title: Half-open: let a few probes through
steps.body: Staying open forever would be a bug. After a cool-down (say 30 seconds) the breaker goes half-open: it lets a few trial calls through, here 3, and holds back everyone else. In the animation all 3 probes succeed, so the breaker closes and normal traffic resumes. In this simple model, if any probe fails, the breaker snaps back to open and the cool-down restarts.
steps.idea: Half-open tests recovery with a trickle, so a healing service is not flooded by the full crowd.
steps.caption: Probes succeed: breaker closes, recs return.

steps.title: Bulkheads cap the blast radius
steps.body: Ships have watertight compartments so one leak cannot sink the hull. Do the same with thread pools. Here Recommendations gets its own limit of 40 concurrent calls out of the 200 threads (normal use is about 20, so there is room for bursts). If it hangs again, only those 40 slots fill and extra recommendation calls are rejected at once. Payments keeps its own pool, so checkout carries on untouched. The breaker will soon trip as well.
steps.idea: A bulkhead caps how much of a shared resource any one dependency may use.
steps.caption: Recs pool full and rejecting; payments unaffected.

steps.title: Where breakers go wrong
steps.body: Breakers can go wrong. They should trip on timeouts and server errors, not client mistakes like 404 or 400. Choose which statuses count (429 and 503 often should). A breaker per instance only sees its own traffic, so a low-traffic caller may never reach the 20-call minimum. A threshold too tight opens on a blip. Too loose reacts late. A silently stale fallback needs alerts so people notice the breaker is open. And never retry a rejection from an open breaker: it only adds load (see Timeouts & Retries).
steps.idea: Breakers need sensible failure definitions, minimum volume, a visible state and a harmless fallback.
steps.caption: Tuning and monitoring decide whether it helps.

steps.title: Fail fast, isolate, degrade
steps.body: A slow dependency exhausts threads, so a timeout turns slowness into a countable failure. The breaker moves closed, then open, then half-open: it stops calling a sick service and tests recovery gently. A bulkhead gives each dependency its own capped pool. A fallback turns a rejected call into a lesser but working answer. Together they keep one broken optional feature from becoming a total outage.
steps.idea: Timeouts detect, breakers stop, bulkheads contain, fallbacks soften.
steps.caption: Page stays up while recommendations are down.

quiz.q: Recommendations goes from 40 ms to hanging for 30 s. Why is that usually more dangerous than it simply being down?
options: Hung calls hold threads and connections, so the caller runs out of capacity
Hung calls use more network bandwidth than refused ones
A hung service writes corrupted data into shared databases
The load balancer removes the caller from rotation immediately
quiz.why: A dead service refuses quickly and frees the thread. A slow one keeps each thread occupied, and at 500 req/s the pool of 200 fills in well under a second.

quiz.q: A breaker is open. What does it do with a new call?
options: Queues it until the dependency recovers
Retries it against the dependency three times
Rejects it immediately, or returns a fallback, without calling the dependency
Sends it to the dependency but ignores the response
quiz.why: Open means the dependency is not contacted. The call returns at once with an error or fallback, which frees the thread and relieves the dependency.

quiz.q: Why does the half-open state allow only a few probe calls rather than all traffic?
options: To measure latency percentiles accurately
To avoid hitting a barely recovered service with full load and knocking it over again
Because half-open only applies to read-only calls
To keep the cache warm
quiz.why: A recovering service may be fragile. A trickle of trial calls tests health cheaply, and a single failure reopens the breaker.

quiz.q: How is a bulkhead different from a circuit breaker?
options: A bulkhead reacts to failure rates; a breaker only counts threads
They are two names for the same mechanism
A bulkhead only works for databases
A bulkhead is a fixed cap on concurrent use per dependency; a breaker reacts to observed failures
quiz.why: The bulkhead is a static limit that works even before failures are measured. The breaker is dynamic and based on outcomes. They are used together.

quiz.q: The checkout 'charge card' call fails. Which fallback is most appropriate?
options: Tell the user clearly that payment could not be completed and let them retry
Report the payment as successful and reconcile later without telling the user
Show a cached list of popular items
Silently skip payment and ship the order
quiz.why: Fallbacks suit optional data. Essential, money-moving operations must not pretend to succeed; the right degradation is an honest error or a retry-safe path.

cheatsheet.def: Normal state. Calls pass through while the breaker counts recent failures in a rolling window.
Tripped state. Calls are rejected immediately or served a fallback; the dependency is left alone.
After a cool-down, a few probe calls test recovery. Success closes the breaker; failure reopens it.
Example only (libraries differ): trip at 50% failures once the window has 20+ calls, stay open 30 s, allow 3 probes. Tune from real traffic.
A breaker needs timeouts to turn hangs into failures it can count. Keep timeouts short.
A per-dependency cap on concurrent calls, threads or connections, so one dependency cannot consume the shared pool.
A cheap substitute answer: cache, default, or hiding the feature. Never use for money-moving writes.
Count timeouts and 5xx errors, often 429 and 503 too, and slow calls if your library supports it. Usually not 4xx client errors like 400 or 404.
